title: A Union Without an Employer: SEWA's Registration in 1972
dek: In 1971 Ela Bhatt listened to the women who hauled cloth through Ahmedabad's market; in 1972 SEWA had to argue that a union needs workers, not an employer.

story.event: Organising self-employed women in Ahmedabad and winning registration as a trade union
story.industry: labour organising (trade union and cooperative finance)
story.summary: In 1971 women who hauled cloth in Ahmedabad's wholesale market asked the women's wing of the Textile Labour Association, led by the lawyer Ela Bhatt, for help with their pay; after a public exchange with the merchants and a meeting of more than a hundred women, the Self-Employed Women's Association was conceived in December 1971. The state Labour Department at first refused to register a union with no employer, but SEWA argued that a union exists to unite workers and was registered on 12 April 1972; its members founded their own cooperative bank in 1974.
paragraphs: In 1971 a group of migrant women who moved cloth through Ahmedabad's wholesale market, pulling handcarts or carrying bolts on their heads, came to the women's wing of the Textile Labour Association for help with their pay. They had no homes and were paid by the load, the head-loaders worst of all. Ela Bhatt, a lawyer who headed the wing, sat with them and heard about contractors who cheated them and work that came and went.

She wrote about their pay in a local newspaper. The cloth merchants replied in print that they paid fair wages. Since the women were not receiving those wages, the wing reprinted the merchants' own claims on small cards and handed them out in the market. Word spread. Used-garment dealers came with grievances of their own, and more than a hundred women met in a park and asked for an association of their own. In December 1971, at the initiative of Bhatt and the union's president, Arvind Buch, the idea of a Self-Employed Women's Association took shape.

The women wanted it to be a trade union. That was new: unions organised employees, and these women had no single employer. By SEWA's own account, the state Labour Department refused to register it, asking whom the workers were organising against. SEWA's answer was that a union exists to unite workers and does not need an employer. The argument held, and on 12 April 1972 SEWA was registered as a trade union, a day it still marks as Self-Employed Day. The Right Livelihood Foundation later called the registration "a formidable hurdle to have surmounted".

Within three years SEWA had more than 5,000 members by the count of the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation in 1977, or 7,000 by the Right Livelihood Foundation's. In 1974 its members started their own cooperative bank, buying shares in it; by 1977 it had over 4,500 shareholders. Bhatt said that the union and the bank had both come "at their insistence". As SEWA's work moved further from the older union's world of mill workers, the Textile Labour Association expelled it and withdrew its support. When Bhatt died in November 2022, aged 90, SEWA had about two million members.

quote.text: for human life is founded on benefits and harmony, and is bound together into an alliance for the common help of all, not by terror, but by love towards one another.
quote.work: Minor Dialogues (On the Shortness of Life, On Tranquillity of Mind, On Anger, On the Happy Life and others)
quote.source_title: Minor Dialogues, Together With the Dialogue on Clemency, tr. Aubrey Stewart, Project Gutenberg eBook #64576
quote.connection: SEWA told the Labour Department that a union exists to bind workers together, not to face an enemy, which is close to Seneca's picture of human life. Yet its first success came from shaming the merchants with their own printed words. Both were true of SEWA at once.

reflection: The Labour Department's question was reasonable by its own rules: a union, as it understood one, was defined by the employer it faced. SEWA did not bend itself to fit the form. It answered with what it was for.

You will be asked questions built for someone else's kind of work, by officials, funders, perhaps by people at home who care about you. The pull is to reshape yourself until the question fits. Before any of this, though, Bhatt sat with the women and listened. Knowing exactly whom you serve is what lets you answer a wrong question calmly.
invitation: Write one sentence that says whom your work is for, rather than what it competes with, and keep it ready for the next time someone asks what you do.

research_notes: Episode changed from the slate. The slate asked for the founding of SEWA Bank in 1974, but the shared web-search budget ran out before a loadable source describing the bank's founding meeting or registration could be found (SEWA Bank's own site has an expired certificate and fails to load; the USAID case study and Bhatt's Seminar essay are unreachable). The story therefore tells the documented founding of SEWA itself in 1971-72, with the bank as its sequel. The detailed 1971 narrative (cloth market, newspaper exchange, cards, park meeting, the Labour Department's reasoning) comes from SEWA's own history page and is signalled as SEWA's account where it matters; Right Livelihood and the Magsaysay Foundation independently confirm the trade-union registration and its difficulty. Membership within three years differs: over 5,000 (Magsaysay biography, 1977) against 7,000 (Right Livelihood); the story gives both with who said what. Bank founding year: SEWA and Right Livelihood give 1974, while The Elders' profile says 1972 in one place and 1973 in its timeline; the story uses 1974. The bank's 4,500-plus shareholders is the Magsaysay Foundation's 1977 figure; Wikipedia's 'began with 4000 women each contributing Rs 10' is not used. SEWA's history gives no date for the TLA's expulsion of SEWA (it says only that tensions had grown by 1981), so the story gives none. Bhatt's age is consistent across sources (39 in 1972 per Magsaysay; died aged 90 in November 2022 per DeshGujarat). Arc remains founding-decision; industry changed from finance to labour organising with cooperative finance. The Seneca passage argues that anger is against human nature; it is applied by analogy to a union defined by solidarity rather than by an opponent.
